submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole detects feminine gender on the token it has just read: it peaks on feminine kinship/role nouns (wife, mother, sister, daughter, woman, girl, lady, queen, actress, goddess), feminine titles and the feminine -ess/-ress suffix (Mrs, Ms, Miss, Princess, baroness, hostess, actress), female given names (Elizabeth, Mary, Lois) and the pronouns she/her/herself, and sits at baseline (~0) on the masculine or gender-neutral token in the same slot (he, him, his, father, brother, son, man, boy, king, actor, host). The trigger is the feminine form itself rather than animacy (it fires on 'She' whose referent is a ship) and strength is graded: frequent kinship nouns, titles and pronouns peak hardest (2.0-3.2), rarer feminine nouns (goddess, waitress, Madam) fire weakly.

For most of the nineteenth century the northern coast was surveyed only in fragments, and the charts that reached the Admiralty were often years out of date. A clerk in the hydrographic office would copy the soundings by hand, compare them against earlier runs, and mark the places where the lead line disagreed with the printed depth. The work was slow, and the office was chronically short of staff. In 1843 a committee recommended a systematic survey of the whole coast from the estuary northward, with fixed stations on the headlands and a chain of signals along the shore so that angles could be taken in clear weather. The recommendation was accepted, though the money arrived in instalments and the first season was lost to storms.

The surveyors worked from small cutters, anchoring overnight in whatever shelter the coast offered. They measured base lines on the beaches with rods, taking care to correct for temperature and for the slope of the sand, and they repeated each measurement until the results agreed to within a few feet. Where the cliffs were too steep for a base line they used a floating log and a measured interval of time, a method that was quick but unreliable in any kind of swell. The records of the early seasons are full of complaints about the weather, the quality of the provisions, and the difficulty of finding men willing to work on the water for the wages offered.

By 1851 the survey had reached the northern islands, and the superintendent reported that the main triangulation was complete. The soundings were another matter. The lead line gave a single depth at a single moment, and the tide ran hard between the islands, so the same spot could read very differently on two consecutive days. The surveyors therefore took their soundings at slack water where they could, and where they could not they noted the hour and the state of the tide beside each figure. This produced a dense and uneven record, difficult to reduce but valuable to later readers, who could reconstruct the conditions under which each measurement had been made.
